headline: Senate bill keeps medical cannabis shield, drops rescheduling freeze
dek: The Senate's FY2027 Justice bill renews protection for state medical programs but omits the House rider that would freeze federal rescheduling work.
key_points: The Senate Appropriations Committee's FY2027 Commerce, Justice, Science bill, posted on 12 November, renews the 2014 rider barring the Justice Department from blocking state medical cannabis laws.
Unlike the House version, the Senate text has no clause stopping federal money from being used to reschedule or deschedule marijuana.
A separate Homeland Security report asks Customs and Border Protection to brief Congress on seizures of state-legal cannabis products within 120 days.
Both chambers must settle their differences, or pass another stopgap, before current federal funding runs out on 11 December 2026.
body: The Senate Appropriations Committee has released a Justice Department funding bill that keeps federal protection for state medical cannabis programs in place and leaves out a House provision that would have frozen the Trump administration's rescheduling work. The fiscal year 2027 Commerce, Justice, Science (CJS) bill was one of five spending bills the committee posted on the evening of 12 November.

For operators, the bill matters in two ways. It renews the shield that has kept federal prosecutors away from state-legal medical businesses since 2014, and it sets up a direct clash with the House over whether Congress should block further moves on marijuana's federal status. The two chambers have until 11 December, when the current stopgap funding law expires, to reach a deal or extend it again.
## What the Senate bill keeps

Section 531 of the Senate text repeats the long-running medical cannabis rider. It bars the Justice Department from spending money to stop listed states, the District of Columbia and four territories from carrying out their own medical marijuana laws, according to the bill language quoted by Marijuana Moment. The list covers 48 states, plus Washington, D.C., Puerto Rico, Guam, the US Virgin Islands and the Northern Mariana Islands, as The Marijuana Herald counted it.

The rider has been federal law since 2014 and has to be carried in each year's spending bill to stay in force, which is why the industry watches it closely every budget cycle. Section 530 also carries forward a separate rider that protects state hemp research programs, created under the 2014 Farm Bill, from interference by the Justice Department or the DEA.
> The quiet win for operators is what the Senate left out: no freeze on rescheduling, and no new school-zone carve-out.
## What the Senate bill leaves out

The House Appropriations Committee approved its own CJS bill in May with two additions the Senate did not copy. The first would bar any money in the bill from being used to reschedule marijuana or remove it from the Controlled Substances Act. The second would state that the Justice Department can still enforce a federal law that raises penalties for distributing cannabis within 1,000 feet of schools, colleges, playgrounds or public housing.

Neither appears in the Senate text, according to Marijuana Moment's review of the bill. That matters because rescheduling is still in progress. The administration moved state-licensed medical marijuana and FDA-approved cannabis drugs to Schedule III by an order that took effect in April, and a DEA hearing is weighing a broader move of all marijuana to Schedule III. A funding ban written into law would have stalled that second step for as long as the bill was in force.

The Congressional Research Service notes that the House committee reported its CJS bill, H.R. 8845, on 15 May with $81.1 billion in total funding. Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins' bill comes in at about $81 billion, according to Bloomberg Government, so the gap between the chambers on cannabis policy is wider than the gap on money.
## Seizures, foreign-linked grows and kratom

The committee reports attached to the bills add three cannabis-related asks. The Homeland Security report directs Customs and Border Protection to brief Congress within 120 days on seizures of cannabis products, and related paraphernalia, held by distributors that comply with state or tribal law. CBP seizures of state-legal products have drawn lawsuits and public criticism from New Mexico Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham, Marijuana Moment reported.

The CJS report asks the Justice Department for a report within 90 days on illegal marijuana grows linked to foreign nationals, including any links to Chinese criminal groups or the Chinese government, and on how federal resources can support state, local and tribal police. The same report asks the DEA for a briefing within 60 days on kratom, after the Department of Health and Human Services referred a kratom byproduct to the DEA for possible scheduling in 2025.
These are report-language requests, not changes in law. They tell agencies what Congress wants to see, and they often signal where enforcement attention will go next.
## How this fits the rest of the Senate package

The CJS bill is the latest piece of a Senate package that has been unusually busy on cannabis. As we reported this morning, reports attached to the Senate's agriculture and veterans bills, released on 10 November, urge a Department of Veterans Affairs study of medical cannabis as an opioid alternative, fund hemp research and raise concerns about cannabis-infused foods. The agriculture draft also kept the 11 December start date for the federal cap of 0.4 milligrams of THC per container on hemp products.

Taken together, the Senate package treats state medical programs as settled and leaves the executive branch free to keep moving on rescheduling, while still pressing agencies on enforcement gaps. The House package takes a harder line on rescheduling. Which approach survives will depend on the final deal.
## The politics behind the numbers

The bills are Republican drafts written for a Congress whose current term ends in January. The midterm elections on 3 November handed Democrats at least 55 Senate seats in the next Congress, according to NBC News. Republicans in both chambers this week chose cannabis opponents Jim Jordan and John Thune as their leaders for the new term, as we reported on 12 November. A spending deal struck in the lame-duck session would set cannabis rules for the rest of fiscal 2027, which runs to 30 September 2027.

The committee has not yet scheduled votes on any of these bills, according to Marijuana Moment, and a full-committee markup that would have covered the CJS bill was postponed in July. Bloomberg Government reported that the Senate bill is unlikely to become law as written, and is mainly meant to set up talks with the House and Democrats.
## What to watch

The first date is 11 December, when the current stopgap funding law expires. Congress must pass full-year bills, another continuing resolution, or face a partial shutdown. The same date is when the second phase of the federal hemp product ban takes effect unless lawmakers change it, so hemp, rescheduling and the medical rider could all be settled in the same end-of-year package.

Watch whether the House's anti-rescheduling clause survives negotiations. If it is dropped, the DEA's broader rescheduling hearing can continue without a funding block. If it is kept, the executive branch would be barred from spending money on further scheduling steps for the rest of the fiscal year. Also watch for the CBP seizure briefing language in a final Homeland Security bill, which would put border-checkpoint seizures of state-legal products on the record for the first time.
